title: Markov Decision Processes: Deciding Over Time
subtitle: Last session's chains told us what happens. Tonight we take the wheel: states, actions, rewards, and policies. The Bellman equation, value iteration, and a tiny shop whose ordering playbook your code writes on its own.

objectives.title: Extend Markov chains with actions and rewards
objectives.description: Move from passive prediction (what will happen) to active control (what should we DO): define states, actions, transition probabilities that depend on your choices, and rewards that make some futures worth more than others.

objectives.title: Build intuition for the Bellman equation
objectives.description: Understand the recursive heart of sequential decision-making: the value of a state equals the best immediate reward plus the discounted value of where you land next. One equation that powers inventory systems, AlphaGo, and every RL algorithm.

objectives.title: Implement value iteration in numpy
objectives.description: Turn the Bellman equation into a working algorithm: iterate values until they converge, extract the optimal policy, and verify it makes business sense on a small inventory problem.

objectives.title: Connect OR to reinforcement learning
objectives.description: Use Warren Powell's 'four classes of policies' framework to see MDPs, stochastic programming, and modern RL as one unified field of sequential decisions — so you can talk to both the operations team and the ML team.

agenda.title: From Watching to Steering
agenda.description: Session 9 was the weather report; tonight you sail. Housekeeping, then the same decision businesses make again and again: a situation, a choice, an uncertain tomorrow, and money on the line. Chat vote: a tiny shop has 1 unit on the shelf and the truck is here. How many do you order?
bulletPoints: Housekeeping: Homework #6 in tonight, no class Nov 25, Homework #7 (pick one) due Dec 2, milestone Dec 9
Sequential decisions everywhere: reorders, airline seats, ride-share drivers, retention discounts, watch-and-wait medicine
Chat vote: 1 unit on the shelf, order 0, 2, 4 or 5? Your code answers it in Part 3

agenda.title: Round 1: Five Words & Notebook Part 1
agenda.description: State, action, chance, reward, policy, plus the patience dial γ. A chain has one transition table; a decision has one table per choice. The gift problem: should a $4 gift go to every customer, none, or only the unhappy ones?
bulletPoints: A policy is a GPS, not printed directions: a best move for every state
Discounting: γ = 0.95 means a business looks about 1 ÷ (1 − γ) = 20 steps ahead
Notebook Part 1: write the gift problem down; the one-month manager never sends a gift

agenda.title: Round 2: The Bellman Equation & Value Iteration (Notebook Part 2)
agenda.description: Plan backward: the fastest drive to New York starts at New York. The Bellman equation in plain English, one step by hand, then value iteration live on the slides: each sweep looks one month further, and at sweep 3 gifting the unhappy starts to pay.
bulletPoints: V(state) = best over choices [ reward now + γ × average V(next state) ]
By hand: gifting an unhappy customer loses $4 today and wins about $1.27 overall
Why not brute force? The shop has 5,598,720 playbooks; value iteration needs about 300 sweeps
Notebook Part 2: value iteration converges in 151 sweeps; checking all 4 playbooks confirms 'gift the unhappy' ($73.66)

agenda.title: Break
agenda.description: Stretch and refuel. You're about to teach a computer to run a shop.

agenda.title: Round 3 Lab: Run the Shop (Notebook Part 3)
agenda.description: The classic inventory MDP. Each morning the shop decides how many units to order, customers arrive at random, sales earn money, and turned-away customers cost goodwill. Build it, run value iteration, read the playbook, and score every order to answer the class vote.
bulletPoints: State 0–10 units, order 0–5, 0–3 customers a day, +$10 a sale, −$8 a unit bought, −$15 per customer turned away, γ = 0.95
Value iteration converges in 292 sweeps; the playbook is 'top up to 3', an order-up-to (base-stock) rule nobody told the code
Vote answer: at 1 unit, order 2 ($56.00), scored with Q(state, action)
A simulated month: the playbook turns no one away; 'order the average' runs out on busy days

agenda.title: Round 4: Turn the Knobs (Notebook Part 4)
agenda.description: A live slider runs value iteration on the slide. Which costs move the playbook? The penalty alone doesn't (a cost only moves the line when it's in a tug-of-war); a $5 truck fee produces 'wait, then fill the truck', the (s, S) pattern; busy days plus a holding cost make the penalty matter.
bulletPoints: Penalty $15 → $40: nothing moves, like a shadow price of zero on a slack constraint
Truck fee $5: order 5 when the shelf is at 2 or fewer; trucks per week 5.25 → 2.10, profit per day −$0.75 → +$1.50 (read from the steady state, Session 9's tool)
Busy days and a $4 holding cost: penalty $15 tops up to 4, penalty $40 to 5
The patience dial: γ = 0.8 vs 0.99 takes 68 vs 1,485 sweeps, same playbook

agenda.title: Powell's Map: Four Classes of Policies
agenda.description: Warren Powell's framework sorts every method for sequential decisions into four kinds: rules of thumb, plans with a buffer, value functions, and lookahead. Tonight is a value function approximation; deep RL is the same idea when the table gets too big.
bulletPoints: PFA (a rule of thumb), CFA (an optimization plan with a buffer), VFA (tonight's V(state)), DLA (think a few moves ahead)
AlphaGo mixed a learned value of each board (VFA) with look-ahead search (DLA)
The curse of dimensionality: 10 products already need 25.9 billion states, so we learn V instead of storing it

activities.title: Teach a Computer to Run a Shop
activities.description: Implement value iteration on a small inventory MDP: a shop with limited shelf space, random daily customers, a purchase cost, and a goodwill penalty for turning customers away. Converge the values, extract the ordering playbook, and discover that your code independently found a classic rule of inventory theory. Then turn the knobs and see which costs actually move it.

steps.title: Describe the shop
steps.description: States: 0–10 units on the shelf. Actions: order 0–5 units, arriving right away (no overfilling the shelf). Customers: 0, 1, 2 or 3 a day, equally likely. Money: +$10 per sale, −$8 per unit bought, −$15 per customer turned away. γ = 0.95.

steps.title: Write the Bellman update
steps.description: For each shelf level and each order, average over the number of customers: today's money plus γ times the value of tomorrow's shelf. Keep the best order.

steps.title: Iterate to convergence
steps.description: Sweep all shelf levels until the largest value change drops below 1e-6 (292 sweeps). Score every order at 1 unit to answer the class vote.

steps.title: Read the playbook, then turn the knobs
steps.description: The playbook is 'top up to 3'. Raise the penalty to $40 (nothing moves — why?), add a $5 truck fee (wait, then fill the truck), and try busy days with a $4 holding cost (now the penalty matters).

codeBlock.code:
import numpy as np

shop = dict(shelf=10, max_order=5, demand=[0, 1, 2, 3], prob=[0.25] * 4,
            price=10, cost=8, penalty=15, gamma=0.95, hold=0, fee=0)

def one_day(shop, stock, order, customers):
    on_shelf = stock + order
    sold = min(on_shelf, customers)
    left = on_shelf - sold
    money = (shop['price'] * sold - shop['cost'] * order
             - shop['penalty'] * (customers - sold) - shop['hold'] * left
             - (shop['fee'] if order > 0 else 0))
    return money, left

def value_iteration(shop, tol=1e-6, **changes):
    shop = {**shop, **changes}               # e.g. value_iteration(shop, fee=5)
    V = np.zeros(shop['shelf'] + 1)
    for sweep in range(1, 100_000):
        V_new, policy = np.zeros_like(V), np.zeros(len(V), dtype=int)
        for s in range(len(V)):
            q = [sum(p * (m + shop['gamma'] * V[left])
                     for d, p in zip(shop['demand'], shop['prob'])
                     for m, left in [one_day(shop, s, a, d)])
                 for a in range(min(shop['max_order'], shop['shelf'] - s) + 1)]
            V_new[s], policy[s] = max(q), int(np.argmax(q))
        if np.max(np.abs(V_new - V)) < tol:
            return V_new, policy, sweep
        V = V_new

V, policy, sweeps = value_iteration(shop)
print(f"Converged in {sweeps} sweeps")          # 292
print("Order at shelf 0..10:", policy.tolist())  # [3, 2, 1, 0, 0, ...]

activities.discussionNote: Your playbook tops the shelf up to 3, the busiest possible day, so no customer is ever turned away. Inventory theorists call this an order-up-to (base-stock) rule; your code found it from five numbers. Now the manager's question: add a $5 delivery fee per truck and re-run. The playbook becomes 'wait until 2 or fewer, then order a full truck', the (s, S) pattern Herbert Scarf proved optimal in 1960. Shelves look fuller (3.5 units at night instead of 1.5) and the CFO frowns. How do you explain it? Trucks per week drop from 5.25 to 2.10 and profit goes from −$0.75 to +$1.50 a day, about $820 a year.

takeaways.text: An MDP = a Markov chain plus actions and rewards. The solution is not a single decision but a policy — a complete state-to-action playbook — and the Bellman equation defines it recursively: best now plus discounted best later.

Value iteration is dynamic programming you can write in about 30 lines of numpy: sweep the Bellman update until values converge, take the best action, and the optimal policy falls out. For the shop it rediscovers the classic order-up-to rule on its own, and a truck fee turns it into the (s, S) rule.

Powell's four classes of policies unify OR and reinforcement learning: deep RL is approximate dynamic programming at scale. When someone says 'we use AI to make decisions,' you now know which of the four policy classes to ask about.

homework.label: Homework #7 · Option A
homework.text: Extend the inventory MDP with holding costs (the Homework #7 shop in the Session 10 notebook, with a wider demand distribution) — one of the two problems you can choose for Homework #7 (the other is the Session 8 pricing curve). Add a charge of $1 per unit of leftover inventory per day (the real cost of tied-up capital and shelf space), re-run value iteration, and compare the optimal policy with and without holding costs side by side. Then answer: (1) How did the order-up-to threshold move, and why? (2) Sweep the holding cost from $0 to $4 and plot the threshold against it. (3) One paragraph for a store manager: in plain English, what tradeoff is the model balancing, and when would carrying 'too much' stock actually be the right call?
